subject: religious-studies
title: The Reformation and the Modern Church
welcome_lead: Travel from Wittenberg in 1517 to Vatican II in 1962, surveying the upheavals that shaped modern Christianity.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the Reformation and Vatican II: Luther, Calvin, Trent, and the ecumenical movement.
final_note: You have traced the Western Church from the Reformation rupture to the modern movements of renewal.

walkthroughs.body_html: Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (1517) attacked indulgences and the financial corruption of late medieval piety. His Freedom of a Christian (1520) expounds justification by faith. John Calvin's Institutes of the Christian Religion (final 1559 edition) systematised Reformed theology around the sovereignty of God, predestination, and the threefold office of Christ as prophet, priest and king.

The Council of Trent (1545-63) reaffirmed seven sacraments, transubstantiation, justification involving infused righteousness, and the authority of tradition alongside scripture. It established seminary training and standardised the Roman liturgy. Often called the 'Counter-Reformation', Trent also reformed clerical abuses internally.

John XXIII opened the Second Vatican Council in 1962 with the aim of aggiornamento (updating). Key documents: Sacrosanctum Concilium (liturgy in the vernacular), Lumen Gentium (church as People of God), Dei Verbum (revelation), Gaudium et Spes (church in the modern world), and Unitatis Redintegratio (ecumenism). The World Council of Churches (1948) had already begun Protestant and Orthodox dialogue.
